p: On the Sunday of the March drill, after Vern told Kit she'd sat the test before, she went back to the dark shop, lifted the foam in her toolbox lid, and took out her 2019 score sheet. From then on it rode in her coat.

At three in the morning at the water plant, the chlorine feed pump lost its prime. Kit bled the gas out of the pump head, read the night's log to see when it had quit, and worked the pounds of chlorine with the plant's formula. The night lead, Leon Yates, asked her to leave it out of the log. It was the third time that month, and he'd kept the first two out himself. She told him to his face she was writing hers, and that his two nights went in the book before the supervisor read it at seven, or she'd tell him she knew. He wrote them before the morning huddle. Driving to Vern's the next night, she thought about how long she'd been leaving one out of her own book.

On Tuesday at Vern's kitchen table she said it plain. In 2019 her Pilot score came back nineteen, and the minimum is twenty five. Boyd had asked her to stay that winter, and she'd said yes because yes was easier than saying nineteen out loud. Then she'd let the shop, her mother, Graham and Boyd himself think it was Boyd, for seven years.

Vern told her about 1973, when he failed the flight physical's eye chart by one line and took the navigator's seat instead. He printed the word from his form, ACUITY, in the margin under her nineteen, the first writing anyone had put on that page. He told her about thirty one years as a freight dispatcher in Kansas City. She gave him the sentence from her letter on an index card, I want to fly, and he stood it against his percolator. Then he showed her an old log where a crew chief grounded a jet his own fuel math said could fly, and she saw that for seven years she'd let a nineteen answer a question nobody had asked her.

That night she told Graham there was a part of 2019 he hadn't heard, that it was hers and not Boyd's, and that she'd tell him all of it on Saturday, April 3, after the practice test. She heard herself say after. He wrote 2019 on the whiteboard in that Saturday's square.

Vern's wife, Patrice, sent Kit home with a gooseberry pie and told her he hadn't talked this much in years. On Saturday in the heritage room Kit asked Vern to keep it until she'd told Graham and Boyd herself. He said he could ask. He said it wasn't his to tell, and it wasn't hers to keep forever. Then, though it was a Saturday and logs came on Tuesdays, he handed her one folded once, and she took it home without opening it.
Corbin Haas. Tech sergeant in the avionics shop, back from chapter two. Two years ago the wing sent him to pilot training, and he washed out and came home to the shop.

Sunday, March 21, a little after five in the morning. Kit had slept four hours and come awake the way the plant had trained her to, all at once, with no reason she could name. Graham was still asleep upstairs. She made coffee in the dark and sat down at the kitchen table in her coat.

The log was in the inside pocket, folded once, on top of the other sheet. It had ridden home on the passenger seat the afternoon before and spent the night in her coat on the hook by the door. Vern gave her logs on Tuesdays, at the end of the night, picked for whatever they'd worked on that week. She'd gone to the heritage room about 2019, and he'd told her it wasn't his to tell and it wasn't hers to keep forever. Then he'd dug in his jacket and handed her this, and he hadn't said what it was for.
She unfolded it under the light over the stove.

My log, nineteen March, oh one. Northbound to the track. Doppler quit at fourteen ten Zulu. True airspeed five hundred. Wind two seven zero at one forty, straight across the course. Drew it on the chart. Steered three four four. Ground speed four eighty. Made good three six zero. Rendezvous on time. Pointed it sixteen left to go straight.
She read it twice. The second time she only read the last line.

She knew crab from the ramp, from watching them come down final on a windy day with the nose pointed off the runway. He'd pointed the nose into the thing pushing him, because that was the only way to go straight. She'd spent seven years pointing away from hers and calling the drift the wing.

The furnace kicked on. Over the table, on the fridge whiteboard, Saturday, April 3, two weeks out, was boxed in green: PRACTICE TEST, 5 HRS, ME ON THE CLOCK. Under that, small, in his black marker, 2019.

Heading and track she knew the way she knew the jet, from outside it. She'd watched a thousand of them go from the cab of her truck at the edge of the ramp, coffee going cold on the dash. Vern had done this one with half his panel dead, at four hundred some knots, and a grease pencil. She dug a sheet of Graham's graph paper out of the junk drawer, under the takeout menus. Course, straight up the page. Wind, square across from the left, 140. The 500 was the airplane through the air, wherever he'd had it pointed.

She put the 500 on the long side, across from the square corner. That was the airplane's own arrow, the one doing the work, and the wind just leaned on it. The wind was a short side. Whatever was left over was the ground. Five hundred squared, 250,000. One forty squared, 19,600. The difference was 230,400, and she worked the root down by guessing: 480. Then she saw it, a little late. Seven times twenty, twenty four times twenty, twenty five times twenty. He hadn't squared a thing. She folded the log back along its crease.

When the wind's square across your course, your own airspeed is the long side, the hypotenuse, across from the right angle. I always drew it before I did a thing, because the drawing tells you which side's which. Wind on one leg, ground speed on the other. Square the long side, take the wind's square off, and find the root. The test's the same deal: find the square corner first. And look for a family. Seven, twenty four, twenty five saved me a lot of squaring in that airplane.

Tuesday at seven the index card was where she'd left it two weeks back, against the percolator, and neither of them said anything about it. Vern didn't mention the Saturday log. She didn't either. It was in her coat on the hook, on top of the other sheet.
He'd seen her graph paper, though, folded in with her homework, the triangle and its three numbers and her arithmetic down the side. He looked at it a while and didn't mark it.
Same airplane. Same wind, two seven zero at one forty. He drew a line straight down a fresh page of the legal pad. Only now you're southbound. Which way does the nose go, Sergeant, and about how far?

The wind came from the west. Southbound, west was on her right. Point a little into it and it would push her back onto the line. Sixteen degrees, same triangle, only the other side of the course: 180 plus 16. She wrote 196. Vern turned the pad around so it faced him and nodded at it. Steer one ninety six, make good one eighty.
After that he put four sets on the table, typed, stapled at the corner. MATH KNOWLEDGE, twenty five apiece. Algebra mostly, then circles and triangles toward the back of each one.

The real one's twenty five of these in twenty two minutes. That's not quite a minute each. He set the egg timer next to the stack and took his hand off it. Practice test is a week from Saturday. How you run these between now and then is yours.

She cranked it to twenty two and went. The algebra went fast. The circles didn't. Twice she put a diameter in where the radius went, and at the bell she was guessing on the last one. Twenty one right. Then she did the four misses over with no clock at all, slowly, and found both diameters in about a minute. Now you know where your time goes, Vern said.
At half past eight he took the pencil from behind his ear and wrote across the top of a clean page.

Spring of ninety nine, the controllers moved our refueling block on us while we were in it. New one was ten miles longer than it was wide, two thousand square miles of sky, and nobody on the radio would tell me the width. There wasn't a thing in that airplane that would do it for me.
Under it, in his capitals: W TIMES THE QUANTITY W PLUS 10 EQUALS 2,000. Factor it the way I did.

She wrote it out the long way first: W squared plus 10W minus 2,000 equals zero. Then she did it his way, the pairs of 2,000 down the margin, 1 and 2,000, 2 and 1,000, 4 and 500, on down, until two of them were ten apart. Forty and fifty. W plus 50, times W minus 40. Forty, or minus fifty, and nobody flies a block of sky minus fifty miles wide. Pairs down the margin, Vern said. Took me about as long as it took you.
Thursday she was on days. Gene had left a note clipped to the board by the door, in his square printing: STICK THE GENSET TANK. ORDER IF UNDER HALF. G.

The plant's backup generator lived in its own shed behind the high service building, a diesel the size of a pickup that ran the pumps when the power went. Its fuel was in a steel tank on cradles beside it, a long cylinder lying on its side, painted gray. She dropped the wooden stick through the fill cap until it touched bottom and pulled it up. Wet to thirty one and three quarter inches.
The chart for it was taped inside the shed door, laminated, gone yellow. The laminate had torn off above the 30 row and under the 33 years ago, and nobody had printed another.

Depth in inches down the side, from thirty to thirty three. Quarter inches across the top. Thirty inches: six sixty seven, six seventy five, six eighty two, six eighty nine. Thirty one: six ninety seven, seven oh four, seven twelve, seven nineteen. Thirty two: seven twenty seven, seven thirty four, seven forty one, seven forty nine. Thirty three: seven fifty six, seven sixty four, seven seventy one, seven seventy nine.

Finger on 31, slide across to the three quarters: 719. Then the neighbors, the way she'd started doing on Vern's tables. 712 before it, 749 right under it, 689 right over it. Then the problem. Under half of what? Nobody had written full down anywhere. The only other thing on paper was a plate riveted to the tank: 6 FT DIA X 8 FT.

Row, then column, then a look at what's around it. That habit is what Table Reading pays for. The neighbors of the right cell are exactly where a slip lands you, and the choices on the test often sit there.
There wasn't a clean sheet of paper in that shed, so she flipped the chart over and used the back, with the pencil that hung off the stick hook on a bootlace.

A drum lying down, really, just a big one. Six feet across and eight end to end, by the plate. Gene wanted half, and in twenty years nobody had worked out what full was. Out the shed door the river was up and brown, carrying half a tree past the intake, and she thought about Yates down there some night soon with his flashlight, cussing at it.

Radius three. Pi times nine times eight, 72 pi. Pi's a little over three, so call it 226 cubic feet. There's 7.48 gallons in a cubic foot, which she knew as well as she knew 8.34, and that made it about 1,692 gallons full, and 846 at half. The stick said 719. She called the fuel dealer from the shed and ordered 950 gallons, a little under what would top it off, and wrote the math on Gene's note under his initial.

A tank lying on its side is a cylinder, and a cylinder is the round end times the length. Round end, pi r squared. The radius is half of six, three. So 9 pi times 8, 72 pi cubic feet. Halve the diameter before anything gets squared. Then the units tell you you're done, cubic feet for a volume.
Saturday morning she took set three to the heritage room. Vern was there on Saturdays, and it was quiet, and nobody but Vern ever came in.

At ten Corbin Haas came in. Jeans, a ball cap, a shoebox under his arm. In the shoebox was the altimeter that had sat on his shelf in February with a yellow tag on it. It had come out of Vern's display case at Christmas, and he'd been at it on his own time since, nights, after the shop cleared out. The needles moved now. He set it on the glass. Don't let anybody tap it. It's older than me. Vern went to the back to find the key to the case, and took his time looking.
Corbin looked at her sheets on the table, the circles and triangles and the egg timer sitting on top of them like a paperweight.

First week, they don't let you near an airplane. It's a classroom and a stack of books, and every one of those books is written from the inside. What's the airplane doing, what do your hands do about it. You know two two eight better than anybody on that ramp. You know it from the outside. You'll walk around it in your head when you ought to be flying it. He tapped the shoebox lid twice, the way you'd knock on a panel to hear if it was loose. The ones who flew in college already think like the airplane. I thought like the guy with the flashlight. Took me a month to quit, and I didn't have a month.

He put his hands in his pockets and looked at the altimeter instead of at her. I called my mom every Sunday night down there. Week five she heard it from a lady at church. I'd talked to her the night before and said fine. He let that sit. So when it quits going fine for you, Darrow, who hears it from you first?

Graham first. Then you, if you'll pick up. Corbin looked at her a long time, long enough that she thought she'd gotten it wrong. Nobody's asked me for anything but the story in two years. He took her pencil and wrote a phone number across the top of set three, over problem one, and gave the pencil back. I'll pick up.

Corbin left a little before eleven. Vern came back with the key just after, which she figured was not an accident, and set the altimeter in the case beside the attitude indicator under the glass. The needles sat at field elevation and stayed there. Vern stood over them with his hands behind his back.
He'd been gone the better part of an hour. The key ring had been on his belt the whole time. She'd seen it when he walked back in.

Thanks for the hour. Vern locked the case and put the key in his shirt pocket. Sergeant Haas has been after me since Christmas to take that thing back. He sat down and pulled set three over to problem fourteen, and that was all either of them said about it.
By the next Tuesday she'd run sets two and three on the egg timer, twenty two minutes each, and reworked the misses slow. Twenty two right, then twenty three. The circles had quit getting her.
Vern didn't spend long on it. He turned the legal pad sideways and printed: W EQUALS 255,000 MINUS 10,000 T.

From my dispatch years. A freighter out of Kansas City turned back twenty minutes out with a hydraulic light, and that model had no way to dump fuel. It was too heavy to put down. W is its weight in pounds after T hours of circling, and the landing limit was two thirty. Under the equation he wrote: W IS AT MOST 230,000.

255,000 minus 10,000 T, at most 230,000. Take the 255,000 over: minus 10,000 T is at most minus 25,000. Divide by minus 10,000 and flip it. T is at least 2.5. Two and a half hours over the river in a holding pattern, Vern said, and the captain called me every one of them. I had another captain once who thought the flip was a suggestion.
Wednesday, a quarter to five, between the plant and supper. Her phone buzzed on the truck seat.
A text from Fisk. Sgt Darrow. Boyd says you're doing my torque retrain at April drill. I've got the study card. Can you look at it before? Don't want to blow it in front of everybody.
She read it at the stop sign by the grain elevator. It was the most words he'd ever put in one text.

She texted back from the stop sign. Thursday, four, the Riverside. Bring the card. You talk. Thursday he was in the back booth in his warehouse shirt with the card face down on the table. She asked questions and didn't answer any. He had the steps in the wrong order once and found it himself, before she said a word, and went red, and went back and did it right. When he was done he looked at her. You didn't tell me a single thing. She paid for his pie. She was halfway home before she noticed she'd done it Vern's way, ask and wait, without deciding to.

Mentoring. A time, a place where nobody's watching, and him doing the work while you ask. You didn't hand him answers, you didn't pass him off, and you didn't save it for the shop floor. The test leans the same way. Develop people by making them do it, privately, soon.

Thursday night, April 1, Graham had a stack of sophomore lab reports and his red pen. Carts let go off a ramp and rolling down the long level bench, distance against time, every graph a little different from the next one.
He slid one across to her without looking up. Two points marked on a straight line, seconds across the bottom, centimeters up the side. The student had written 1/15 at the bottom for the speed.
You've got Saturday on your mind. Do one for me anyway. What should it say?
Behind him on the whiteboard, under Saturday's green box, was the 2019 he'd written. Neither of them had looked at it all week, which in that kitchen took some doing.

She took the two points the long way, the way Vern would have. Ninety less thirty, sixty. Six less two, four. Fifteen centimeters a second, and the student had it upside down. Graham wrote it on the paper in red and drew a little arrow at the line. That's what I keep telling them. The slope's the speed. She nodded. He went back to the stack.

Up 60, over 4, slope 15. On a distance and time graph that's the speed, so it carries units, centimeters a second here. Graham tells his sophomores the same thing. Subtract both points in the same order and the sign looks after itself.

Friday night the whiteboard came off the fridge again. It slid off its bracket while Graham was writing 8:00 into Saturday's box, and the marker went down the whole week in one long green line. He laughed at it. Bracket. Again. He pinned it to the fridge with his palm, still grinning. Eight o'clock. I'll call time at the end of every block, and I won't say anything else.
She went out for the drill. The light in the garage came on by itself when she opened the side door, the way it always did.

The drill was on the pegboard. Its battery wasn't. She tried behind the mower. Graham had pulled the mower out on Sunday for the first cut of the year and shoved it back in crooked, and one corner of the blue tarp had come up with the handle.
Under the corner was a rail. Pale wood, worn smooth, with round spindles under it, close together.

She lifted the tarp. A crib. Maple, from the color, with the mattress board bare and a paper tag tied to one post with string. SOLD, in grease pencil, and a date. April 2025. Two springs ago. The KC-46 talk had just started that spring, and he'd stood at this same door and asked her whether this could be the year, and she'd said after.

She put her hand on the rail. Somebody else's hands had rubbed it pale long before it ever got here. Graham's whiteboard stopped at May, at its aluminum edge. She'd seen that in February and hadn't asked, and now she knew what he'd kept off it.
She put the tarp back. She put it back the way it had been, the corner under the mower handle, and that took longer than it should have.
She'd given him Saturday herself, all of 2019 with the paper on the table. And he'd had this out here two springs, under a tarp, and never once asked her to come and look.
She left it. His was his. Hers came first, and it was seven years overdue, and she wasn't going to ask him for anything until she'd set it down in front of him. After that, the tarp was his to lift.
The battery was in the jar of screws on the shelf, same as February, under a handful of drywall anchors nobody in this house had ever used. She stood there holding it.

Tomorrow night, then. Kitchen table, the sheet out of her coat, and hers said first, all of it, before anybody touched that tarp. She had the battery so tight in her fist the edge was biting her. In the kitchen Graham would still be holding the whiteboard to the fridge with one hand, reading Saturday off it, waiting on her and the drill.

Graham had put that light up himself, the summer they bought the place, and set it on two minutes because one wasn't enough to find your keys. Two minutes went by. Nothing in the garage moved, so it clicked off on her.
